lines.text: A Japanese plane is pulled toward you, just like the saw. A thin shaving curls up out of the block.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: This time, the rest of the cutting kit: chisels, the hammer, and the plane.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Japanese chisels, nomi, come in two families. Tataki-nomi are struck with a hammer. Tsuki-nomi are pushed by hand, and are used for finishing.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: Japanese chisels, noh-mee, come in two families. Tah-tah-kee noh-mee are struck with a hammer. Tsoo-kee noh-mee are pushed by hand, and are used for finishing.

lines.text: A struck chisel has an iron hoop fitted around the end of its handle. Carpenters call it the katsura.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: A struck chisel has an iron hoop fitted around the end of its handle. Carpenters call it the kah-tsoo-rah.

lines.text: The general bench chisel is the oire-nomi. For deep mortises there is the mukōmachi-nomi, with a thick, heavy blade, made for chopping straight down into the wood.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The general bench chisel is the oh-ee-reh noh-mee. For deep mortises there is the moo-koh-mah-chee noh-mee, with a thick, heavy blade, made for chopping straight down into the wood.

lines.text: Now look at the blade itself. Like most Japanese edge tools, a chisel is bevelled on one side only. A thin layer of very hard steel, hagane, is forge-welded to a softer iron body, jigane. The hard steel holds the edge; the softer iron supports it.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: Now look at the blade itself. Like most Japanese edge tools, a chisel is bevelled on one side only. A thin layer of very hard steel, hah-gah-neh, is forge-welded to a softer iron body, jee-gah-neh. The hard steel holds the edge; the softer iron supports it.

lines.text: The back of the blade has a shallow hollow, the urasuki. It makes the back easier to keep perfectly flat. The bevel itself stays flat, not hollow-ground.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The back of the blade has a shallow hollow, the oo-rah-soo-kee. It makes the back easier to keep perfectly flat. The bevel itself stays flat, not hollow-ground.

lines.text: The hammer is the gennō. One face is flat. The other is slightly domed. It's commonly used to strike chisels, as well as for nails.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The hammer is the gen-noh. One face is flat. The other is slightly domed. It's commonly used to strike chisels, as well as for nails.

lines.text: Driving a nail, you strike with the flat face, then give the last blows with the domed face, so the surface isn't marked. That face is the kigoroshi face: literally, the wood-crushing face.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: Driving a nail, you strike with the flat face, then give the last blows with the domed face, so the surface isn't marked. That face is the kee-goh-roh-shee face: literally, the wood-crushing face.

lines.text: The plane is the kanna. Like the saw, it's pulled toward you, with both hands. Western and Chinese planes are pushed.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The plane is the kahn-nah. Like the saw, it's pulled toward you, with both hands. Western and Chinese planes are pushed.

lines.text: The blade sits in a wooden block, the dai, usually of hard oak. There is no screw. In the skills test manual, the blade is set with light taps of a hammer: on the blade's head to advance it, on the block to draw it back.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: The blade sits in a wooden block, the dye, usually of hard oak. There is no screw. In the skills test manual, the blade is set with light taps of a hammer: on the blade's head to advance it, on the block to draw it back.

lines.text: Most have a second iron behind the blade: the chip breaker, uragane. It helps stop tearing in difficult grain. This two-blade plane dates from the Meiji era.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.
lines.tts: Most have a second iron behind the blade: the chip breaker, oo-rah-gah-neh. It helps stop tearing in difficult grain. This two-blade plane dates from the May-jee era.

lines.text: If you work with Western tools, the jobs are the same: bench chisels, a hammer or mallet, a bench plane. The plane is the clearest difference. It's pushed, and the blade is held by a wedge or a screw.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Every one of these tools depends on a sharp edge. The skills test manual is blunt about it: a dull tool invites injury. Keep chisels and planes sharp, and never point an edge at yourself or anyone else.
lines.instr: A calm, warm, unhurried documentary narrator teaching a hand craft to a friend. Slow, steady pace of about 130 words per minute, with a short natural pause after each sentence. Japanese words are pronounced the Japanese way: even syllables, pure vowels, no English stress.

lines.text: Strike the chisel, or push it. Pull the plane. And keep every edge sharp.

lines.text: One note: sharp-tool technique, and how to use these tools safely, is best learned from a teacher, at a bench, in person.
